intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is caused by homozygous mutation in the Na+/glucose cotransporter gene SGLT1 (SLC5A1) on chromosome 22q13.1.

checks.explanation: The paper names SLC5A1 as the causal gene, and the abstract reports homozygous mutations in affected individuals.

paragraphs.text: Glucose/galactose malabsorption is an autosomal recessive disorder in which the intestine selectively fails to absorb dietary glucose and galactose. It begins within the first weeks of life with severe diarrhea and dehydration, which are usually fatal unless these sugars are removed from the diet (Turk et al., 1991). Absent intestinal glucose transport may be accompanied by partial impairment of renal glucose transport (Elsas et al., 1970).

checks.evidence_quote: Glucose/galactose malabsorption (GGM) is an autosomal recessive disease
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.evidence_quote: characterized by a selective failure to absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Glucose/galactose malabsorption begins within the first weeks of life with severe diarrhea and dehydration.
checks.evidence_quote: manifesting within the first weeks of life and characterized by a selective failure to absorb dietary glucose and galactose from the intestine. The consequent severe diarrhoea and dehydration
checks.explanation: Onset and the main symptoms are both stated.

checks.claim: The severe diarrhea and dehydration of glucose/galactose malabsorption are usually fatal unless glucose and galactose are removed from the diet.
checks.evidence_quote: The consequent severe diarrhoea and dehydration are usually fatal unless these sugars are eliminated from the diet.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) studied a 3-year-old girl with congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption and her family. In vitro, her jejunal mucosa could not concentrate glucose at any point during a 60-minute incubation. In contrast, mucosa from 6 normal controls and from her asymptomatic 5-year-old brother accumulated glucose to 16 times its concentration in the incubation medium. Fructose accumulation was similar in all subjects. Renal glucose titration showed a partial defect in renal glucose reabsorption in the proband. Her brother's titration curve was similar to those of 7 normal volunteers.

paragraphs.text: Abdullah et al. (1996) described 8 Arab children from 8 different families with glucose-galactose malabsorption. Six were Saudi Arabs and 2 were of other Arab nationalities. The mean age at presentation was 10.6 months. All had chronic watery diarrhea from birth and failure to thrive. Small-bowel biopsy, histology, and small-bowel enzyme assay confirmed the diagnosis. One child had a renal stone at the first visit, and another was found to have one at follow-up.

paragraphs.text: Xin and Wang (2011) reported 33 patients with GGM from a large Old Order Amish pedigree. All presented with classic watery diarrhea and dehydration. The initial presentation also included increased bowel sounds, distended abdomen, vigorous nursing despite illness, and irritability and apathy. When the disease was correctly diagnosed and adequately managed, the diarrhea stopped immediately, rehydration was quick, and growth and development were normal afterward. When the disease was not recognized, the clinical course was prolonged.

paragraphs.text: Elsas et al. (1970) found that glucose transport by normal human jejunal mucosa was concentrative, saturable, sodium and energy dependent, and showed competitive inhibition. Both parents and a half sister of their proband had impaired mucosal glucose transport, with values between normal and those of the proband. In these 3 heterozygotes, glucose influx was impaired, but glucose efflux matched that in 3 normal controls. Kinetic analysis showed a reduced capacity (Vmax) but a normal affinity (Km) for glucose transport.

paragraphs.text: In members of a family with GGM, Turk et al. (1991) amplified SGLT1 cDNA and genomic DNA by PCR and sequenced the products. Turk et al. (1993) stated that the mutation in their 2 patients was an asp28-to-asn change, which eliminated SGLT1 transport activity in vitro.

agent.process_note: I read all 11 files in full. Six are abstracts only and four are titles only. Turk et al. (1991) shows the gene to be SGLT1/SLC5A1, and Turk et al. (1993) places it at 22q13.1. The reference data gave no gene MIM number, so none is written. The specific D28N change comes from Turk 1993 and Martin 1996 (Prenat Diagn), not from the Turk 1991 abstract. The Martin 1996 Nat Genet abstract names no individual mutations. No paper reports compound heterozygosity. The four Amish variants of Xin and Wang (2011) are listed separately, as reported; the abstract does not say which of them is causal. The four title-only papers are cited only for what their titles say.
